title: Pronouns and possessives
tagline: I, me, my, mine: pronouns and possessives for people and things.
why: Pronouns save you from repeating names all the time, and possessives show who owns what — both come up in almost every sentence you say or write. Reading Part 6 loves testing whose, mine and each other because one small word changes the whole meaning.

hook.text: Miss Vega opens the lost property box. "Whose jacket is this?" she asks. "It's not mine," says Liam. "Mine is red." "I think it's Nadia's," says Sofia.
hook.ask: Mine and Nadia's both show who owns something, but they work in different ways. Can you see how?

watch_out.why: Use subject pronouns before the verb, not object pronouns.
Mine already means 'my book' — never add 's to a possessive pronoun.

watch_out.wrong: Whose is this jacket? It's Liam.
watch_out.why: You need the apostrophe s to show it belongs to Liam.

watch_out.wrong: I need a new one shoes.
watch_out.why: Ones replaces a plural noun — no a before it.
When the action comes back to the same person, use a reflexive pronoun.

l1.why: Before a verb, English needs subject pronouns, even when Spanish word order feels different.
My always needs a noun after it; mine stands alone.
Spanish se often becomes a reflexive pronoun like himself in English, not him.
Whose asks about ownership; who asks about a person's identity.

remember.trick: MY needs a noun. MINE stands alone!
remember.tip: If a noun comes right after the word, it's my/your/her. If the word stands by itself, it's mine/yours/hers.

can_do: I can use subject pronouns (I, she) and object pronouns (me, her) correctly.
I can choose between my and mine, and use 's to show who something belongs to.
I can use one/ones, myself/each other and words like someone/anywhere.
summary: Subject pronouns (I, she, they) go before the verb; object pronouns (me, her, them) go after it.
My, your, her + noun; mine, yours, hers alone — never add 's to mine, yours or hers.
Add 's to show who owns something: Sofia's bag; ask with whose.
One/ones replace a noun, reflexive pronouns (myself) show the action comes back, and each other means one to the other.
